issues.legal_issue: A written instrument recording a gift under Muhammadan law does not invariably require registration merely because it is written or contemporaneous with the gift.
material_facts: The dispute concerned an instrument executed in connection with an alleged gift of immovable property under Muhammadan law.

The lower courts treated the instrument as evidence of an earlier oral gift, while the High Court treated it as an instrument transferring the property in the present and therefore requiring registration.

The Supreme Court held that the nature and registration requirement of a written instrument depend on the circumstances, but did not need to determine registration in this case because the alleged gift was incomplete for want of possession.
issues.conclusion: A written instrument relating to a Muhammadan gift is not invariably required to be registered; writing alone does not determine whether registration is required. The question of registration did not arise on these facts because the gift was incomplete for want of possession.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 123 and 129 of the Transfer of Property Act distinguish the general registration requirement for gifts of immovable property from the saving of Muhammadan law. Section 17 of the Registration Act does not apply categorically to every written Muhammadan gift. Applying Hafeeza Bibi v. Shaikh Farid, Nasib Ali v. Wajid Ali, and Mahboob Sahab v. Syed Ismail, the Court held that the character and registration requirement of the writing depend on the facts; the essential requirements of a valid Muhammadan gift must still be fulfilled.

predicates.muhammadan_gift_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a gift made under Muhammadan law is valid.
predicates.gift_is_recorded_in_writing: The alleged gift is recorded in a written instrument.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns a Muhammadan gift recorded in writing, the writing alone does not make registration mandatory.

issues.legal_issue: A gift of immovable property under Muhammadan law is incomplete unless the donor declares the gift, the donee accepts it, and possession is delivered actually or constructively to the donee.
material_facts: The alleged donor's written instrument described him as the owner in possession and did not support the claim that an earlier oral gift had been made.
The alleged donee was not shown to have lived at the property with the donor and the evidence indicated that she lived elsewhere with her husband.
No rent receipts showed that she collected rent from tenants; receipts showed the donor continued to issue them after the instrument was executed.
The property had not been mutated in her favour, and she did not possess the title deeds.
The evidence therefore did not establish either actual possession or constructive possession by the alleged donee.
issues.conclusion: The alleged gift was not complete because the alleged donee had not proved actual or constructive possession. The Supreme Court affirmed the High Court's judgment and dismissed the appeal, leaving the suit dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Muhammadan law, a valid gift requires declaration by the donor, express or implied acceptance by the donee, and delivery of possession actually or constructively. Sections 149, 150 and 152 of Mulla's Principles of Mahomedan Law describe these requirements, including the need for an overt act showing transfer of possession where donor and donee reside together. Valia Peedikakkandi Katheessa Umma v. Pathakkalan Narayanath Kunhamu recognizes the importance of actual or constructive possession. Possession may be shown by control over the property, as described in section 394 of Tyabji's Muslim Law. Mahboob Sahab v. Syed Ismail and Hafeeza Bibi v. Shaikh Farid also state the essential requirements of a valid gift.

issues.definition: When a proceeding concerns the validity of a Muhammadan gift and the donee did not prove actual or constructive possession, the gift is incomplete and invalid.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere under Article 136 with concurrent factual findings that are manifestly perverse or unsupported by the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court found that an earlier oral gift had been made, although the written instrument described the alleged donor as remaining owner in possession and the record did not support the finding.

The lower courts inferred that the alleged donee had possession, but the evidence, including residence records, rent receipts, mutation records and title documents, did not support actual or constructive possession.
The Supreme Court scrutinized the evidence and rejected the concurrent findings as contrary to the record.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court was entitled to reassess and interfere with the concurrent factual findings because they were manifestly unsupported by the evidence.
issues.legal_principle: In exercise of its jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court can interfere with concurrent findings of fact when the conclusions are manifestly perverse or unsupported by the evidence. The Court relied on Alamelu v. State, Heinz India (P) Ltd. v. State of U.P., and Vishwanath Agrawal v. Sarla Vishwanath Agrawal.

issues.definition: When a special leave appeal challenges concurrent factual findings that are manifestly perverse or unsupported by the evidence, the Supreme Court may interfere with those findings.
